extracted.intended_audience: students, natural philosophers, and scientists interested in scientific method and reasoning
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance on the use, limits, and verification of generalisation and analogical reasoning in scientific inquiry, including cautions about discontinuities, hasty inference, and examples of productive analogical transfer between fields.

rubrics_metrics.name: Principle of Continuity (Law of Continuity)
rubrics_metrics.description: The 'Law of Continuity' is a principle of nature holding rigorously true in many relations of natural forces but whose limits are difficult to assign.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply the law carefully: many phenomena appear discontinuous (e.g., total internal reflection, negative magnetism) even where underlying theories (e.g., undulatory theory) show continuity. Exercise caution in extending continuity across domains; identify singular points where laws change (example: gravitational force inside, outside, and on the surface of a spherical shell shows double discontinuity).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use continuity for negative arguments (refutation by ad infinitum consequences)
rubrics_metrics.description: Arguments based on continuity can show a hypothesis impossible if it entails continual repetition ad infinitum or requires a purely arbitrary breach at some point.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such negative arguments effectively refute theories that imply infinite regress or perpetual motion (examples: Bonnet's preformation theory generating infinite nested germs; Stevinus's endless chain producing perpetual motion; Newton's reasoning for equality of action and reaction). These are powerful but must be applied with awareness of their assumptions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limitations of continuity-based proofs
rubrics_metrics.description: Continuity arguments cannot absolutely prove some large-scale conservation laws (e.g., conservation of energy); they may show probability rather than absolute truth.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognise that continuity-based reasoning can be suggestive but not conclusive; question background assumptions (e.g., whether past time is infinite or matter creation/destruction behaviours). Do not treat such arguments as final proof without further justification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Beware of hasty generalisation
rubrics_metrics.description: Humans are prone to drawing hasty and ill-considered inferences from limited cases; early inductions are often imperfect and inconclusive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cultivate caution and discrimination: generalisation requires long training and repeated verification. Avoid inferring broad laws from isolated or superficial resemblances; the faculty to generalise accurately develops with experience and careful approximation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid false numerical and superficial analogies
rubrics_metrics.description: Superficial numerical analogies (e.g., mystical importance of the number seven) can mislead and produce false generalisations and superstitions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not infer deep causal or structural relations solely from shared numerical features; historical examples (seven metals/planets/tones) show how number-based analogies produced baseless theories. Test whether resemblance is substantive or merely superficial.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not assume nature always prefers simplicity (caution about simplicity axioms)
rubrics_metrics.description: The axiom that 'nature proceeds in the simplest way' may be questionable and does not necessarily apply to proximate laws; simplicity is agreeable but not decisive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: While simplicity is heuristically useful, avoid using it as an unquestioned principle for selecting hypotheses. Even if ultimate laws are simple, proximate results can be complex; verify rather than assume simplicity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Power and required caution of generalisation
rubrics_metrics.description: Generalisation is the great prerogative of the intellect and a chief source of scientific advance, but it must be exercised with much caution and after long training.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Seek deep and carefully verified resemblances; successful generalisations (e.g., Copernican system) often overturn shallower generalisations. Verify generalisations across varied conditions and resist overextension beyond the verified domain.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish generalisation from analogy
rubrics_metrics.description: Generalisation involves viewing many objects as agreeing in a few properties (resemblance extensive rather than deep); analogy is reasoning from a few objects that present many points of resemblance (deeper correspondence of relations).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the distinction to choose methods: generalisation supports broad inductive rules; analogy supports targeted hypotheses about deeper relational correspondences. Be aware of vagueness in terms but keep the operational distinction in mind when designing inference or experiments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Analogy as resemblance of relations (not merely things)
rubrics_metrics.description: Analogy often denotes a resemblance between the relations of things (e.g., pilot:ship :: prime minister:state) rather than identity of the things themselves.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When arguing by analogy, map relational structure carefully and check which relations correspond. Avoid conflating analogy of roles/relations with identity of nature or properties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Degrees of analogy and strength of inference
rubrics_metrics.description: Analogy exists in degrees: from mere similarity of number or ratio to deep resemblances of physical properties (e.g., iodine and chlorine).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess how many and how substantial the corresponding properties are before inferring from one case to another. Greater and deeper-pointwise correspondence increases confidence; superficial resemblances warrant only tentative hypotheses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use analogy as a heuristic guide in discovery
rubrics_metrics.description: Analogy frequently provides the first clue in discovery; when faced with many possible experiments or hypotheses, follow the most probable course suggested by analogy rather than random trial.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Select experimental paths inspired by analogies to known phenomena (examples: chemist treating a new element like known alkali metals; Herschel anticipating magneto-optical effects from analogies). Follow analogical leads but verify results empirically.

rubrics_metrics.name: Verify analogical inferences by experiment
rubrics_metrics.description: Analogical conclusions must be tested; analogical expectation does not substitute for empirical confirmation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Historical instances (Herschel's anticipation of Faraday's effect; his own experiments converting probability into certainty in related cases) show the need for experimental validation. Treat analogy as hypothesis-generation, not proof.

rubrics_metrics.name: Seek analogies across mathematical and scientific branches to generate methods
rubrics_metrics.description: Discovering analogies between branches (e.g., geometry and algebra) enables transfer of methods, unlocking new developments and discoveries.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Look for structural correspondences that permit applying techniques from one domain to another (examples: Descartes uniting algebra and geometry; Boole connecting logic and algebra). Use analogy deliberately to create new tools and generalisations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Define domain of applicability for laws; avoid overextension
rubrics_metrics.description: A law that holds in one domain may change abruptly at singular points or in different contexts (example: gravitational law outside vs. inside a spherical shell).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When proposing or applying a law, specify its limits and check for singular cases where a different law may govern. Avoid treating phenomena under one law if they belong to different laws; test boundary cases explicitly.
